growth_story.headline: Kuwait's income per person is 63.7 percent below its 1971 peak; since 1990, war, oil slumps and OPEC+ output cuts have kept knocking back its oil economy.
growth_story.arc: Kuwait's income per person peaked in 1971, and in 2025 it was 63.7 percent below that level and lower than in 1970, the first year of the record. The 1990–1997 era averaged 7.8 percent a year, but it was mostly a rebound: Iraq's invasion cut income per person by 26.5 percent in 1991, then oil infrastructure was quickly restored and the population shrank, so it jumped 51.1 percent in 1992. The 1998–2007 era averaged 2.6 percent: income per person jumped 14.6 percent in 2003, and from 2004 a world boom, a calmer region and rising oil prices lifted the economy, though the gains per person had faded by 2007. The 2008–2017 era averaged -4.0 percent: the global financial crisis and lower oil prices and output brought an 11.9 percent fall in 2009, lower oil prices later strained public finances, and OPEC+ output cuts led to an 8.2 percent fall in 2017. Since 2018 the average has been -0.9 percent, with new OPEC+ cuts behind a 7.0 percent fall in 2023 and their unwinding behind a 3.4 percent rise in 2025.

threads.title: OPEC+ quotas set the pace
threads.text: Kuwait's oil output follows quotas agreed with other OPEC+ producers, so its growth swings with those joint decisions. Cuts pulled the economy down in 2017 and 2023, and unwinding them drove the 2025 recovery.

since_last_year.text: In 2025 the economy recovered as OPEC+ output cuts were unwound, and income per person rose 3.4 percent. Then the 2026 Middle East conflict closed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and damaged key infrastructure. The World Bank now expects a deep contraction in 2026, and in September 2026 the government allowed borrowing from its Future Generations Fund for the first time in decades.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes 2004–08 as a time of strong economic growth, fed by a world boom and rising oil prices. Income per person tells a weaker story. It rose 7.8 percent in 2004 and 6.7 in 2005, was flat by 2007 (-0.1) and fell 3.1 percent in 2008, because the population was growing fast too and shared the gains. The early 1990s run the other way. The IMF says the economy as a whole took seven years to regain its pre-war size, yet income per person was above its pre-war level within two years because the population shrank. So the 7.8 percent average for 1990–1997 reflects a rebound and fewer people, not a long boom.
